clinicalPearls: A drug-induced eruption confined to light-exposed skin, typically the face, V of the neck, dorsa of the hands and extensor forearms, with sparing of shaded sites
Reactions divide into phototoxic, which are common, dose-dependent and resemble exaggerated sunburn, and photoallergic, which are immune-mediated, eczematous and affect only sensitised individuals
The action spectrum is usually within the ultraviolet A range, so reactions can occur through window glass and despite ultraviolet-B-blocking sunscreens
Frequently implicated systemic drugs include certain thiazide diuretics, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, amiodarone, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and voriconazole
Sparing of the upper eyelids, submental region and skin behind the ears helps confirm a photodistributed pattern
Some drugs cause distinctive patterns such as photo-onycholysis, a lichenoid photoreaction, or pseudoporphyria with skin fragility and blistering
Chronic amiodarone or long-term photosensitisers can produce slate-grey pigmentation of exposed skin
Management is withdrawal or substitution of the culprit drug where possible, strict broad-spectrum photoprotection and topical corticosteroids for symptomatic skin
reference.pathophysiology: Photodistributed drug eruptions arise when a systemic drug or its metabolite absorbs ultraviolet radiation in the skin. In phototoxic reactions the absorbed energy generates reactive oxygen species and other cytotoxic photoproducts that directly damage keratinocytes and other cutaneous cells, producing an exaggerated sunburn-like response that depends on the dose of both drug and light and can occur on first exposure. In photoallergic reactions the drug is converted by light into a photoproduct that acts as a hapten, provoking a delayed type IV, T-cell-mediated hypersensitivity that requires prior sensitisation and produces an eczematous eruption. The predominance of ultraviolet A in the action spectrum explains why reactions occur despite ordinary sunscreens and through glass.
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic photodermatoses such as polymorphic light eruption and chronic actinic dermatitis
Photoallergic and phototoxic contact reactions from topical agents
Porphyria cutanea tarda and drug-induced pseudoporphyria
Pellagra and other nutritional photosensitive dermatoses
additionalInvestigations: Detailed drug and sun-exposure history correlating onset with photosensitising medication
Assessment of the distribution to confirm sparing of shaded sites
Phototesting to define the action spectrum and photopatch testing to identify photoallergy
Skin biopsy in atypical cases to distinguish phototoxic, lichenoid or pseudoporphyria patterns
Porphyrin studies to exclude true porphyria in blistering presentations
Autoimmune serology to exclude photosensitive lupus
redFlags: Blistering with skin fragility suggesting pseudoporphyria or true porphyria
Progression toward persistent light sensitivity or chronic actinic dermatitis
An essential photosensitising drug that cannot easily be withdrawn, requiring specialist input
Features raising the possibility of cutaneous or systemic lupus
reference.prognosis: Most reactions resolve after the culprit drug is stopped and light exposure minimised, though phototoxic pigmentation and drug-induced photosensitivity can persist for a time after withdrawal, and rarely a lasting photosensitivity develops.
pitfalls: Attributing a photodistributed eruption to a topical product while missing a systemic photosensitising drug
Advising only ultraviolet-B sunscreens when the reaction is driven by ultraviolet A
Failing to recognise pseudoporphyria and confusing it with true porphyria
Overlooking the sparing of shaded sites that defines the photodistributed pattern
references: British Association of Dermatologists guidance on drug-induced photosensitivity
management: Withdraw or substitute the culprit photosensitising drug, such as a thiazide, tetracycline, fluoroquinolone, amiodarone, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug or voriconazole
Enforce photoprotection with broad-spectrum UVA sunscreen, protective clothing and sun avoidance, recognising reactions occur through window glass
Treat the eczematous photoallergic component with topical corticosteroids and give supportive care for the sunburn-like phototoxic reaction
Investigate blistering presentations with porphyrin studies to exclude pseudoporphyria and true porphyria
Where the drug is essential, adjust dosing and timing or select a non-photosensitising alternative in consultation with the prescriber
Monitor for resolution and for residual pigmentation or persisting photosensitivity after withdrawal
